one_liner: Single-header C99 float FFT (0BSD), scalar radix-8 mixed-radix, 1.1-1.5x faster than KissFFT on power-of-two sizes.
what_it_does: meow_fft is one 2,343-line C99 header with forward and inverse complex FFTs (meow_fft, meow_fft_i) and real-input FFTs (meow_fft_real, meow_fft_real_i), single precision only. You call a generate_workset function once with NULL to get a byte size, allocate that many bytes yourself, call it again to fill the plan, and then pass the plan to the out-of-place transform calls. It is not a drop-in for KissFFT: the plan layout, the real-FFT output packing and the function names all differ.
how_it_is_fast: It is a recursive decimation-in-time mixed-radix FFT that factors N greedily by 8, 5, 4, 3 and 2. Each stage's twiddles are precomputed in the order they are read. The author says the radix-8 butterfly, generated with FFTW's codelet generator, is the only reason it beats KissFFT. The real-input transform runs a half-length complex FFT and then a symmetric post-processing mix (the two-for-one trick). The code uses no explicit SIMD.
when_to_use: You want a GPL-free FFT as one 0BSD file with no build system, and KissFFT is what you would use otherwise
Power-of-two float transforms from about 256 to 32768 points (for example audio frames): the author's i7-4790 table shows 1.07-1.50x over KissFFT, and gemmi measured 1.2-1.5x at n=256 and 512
Targets where SIMD code is unavailable or unwanted (scalar builds, WebAssembly without SIMD, ARMv7): on a 1 GHz ARMv7 the author measured 1.1-1.75x over KissFFT for N=64-32768
Reading a compact, commented mixed-radix FFT to learn how one is put together (one of the author's stated goals)
when_not_to_use: Whenever a SIMD FFT is allowed: pffft ran N=1024 in 2.19 us against meow's 8.89 us (i7-4790), and muFFT, FFTW and vDSP are also faster according to the author

When a scalar FFT faster than KissFFT is enough: in gemmi's C2C run, PocketFFT (scalar, double precision) and pffft or FFTW with SIMD disabled all beat meow at every size tested (for example n=256: 1690-1826 ns against 2120 ns)
Very small or non-power-of-two sizes: KissFFT is faster at N=64 (0.58 against 0.73 us), level or faster at N=100 and 500, and faster for gemmi's real FFT at n=480 (3140 against 3591 ns)
Sizes with prime factors other than 2, 3 and 5: radix 7 and larger primes go through an O(p^2) generic DFT, and a prime factor above 2048 aborts the process
Double precision, 2D/3D transforms, odd-length real FFTs or in-place transforms: none is supported

integration.min_toolchain: C99 (also compiles as C++ via extern "C" guards); MSVC before VS2022 (_MSC_VER < 1930) gets a volatile work-around for optimiser bugs
integration.platforms: any (portable scalar C); author benchmarked x86-64 (i7-4790, Core2 Duo P8400) and ARMv7
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the transforms take the plan as const and keep no global state (scratch is on the stack or in caller buffers), so one plan can probably be shared across threads

gotchas: The real FFT writes N/2 complex values and stores the Nyquist bin's real part in out[0].j. The header comment still says countof(out) == countof(in), which predates the July 2024 change, and issue #14 (open) asks how to read the output. Inverse transforms are not scaled, so divide by N yourself.

The plan generator accepts any N >= 2 (complex), or any even N >= 4 (real), and returns 0 otherwise. A prime factor above 2048 is not rejected at plan time: meow_dft_n_dit calls abort() during the transform (for example N = 4099). meow_fft_is_slow() reports when the slow generic DFT will be used.

The plan is one caller-allocated block holding absolute pointers into itself, so do not memcpy or realloc it; allocate it where it will live. The internal helpers (meow_radix_2_dit, meow_add and others) have external linkage, and several are plain C99 `inline`, so define MEOW_FFT_IMPLEMENTATION in exactly one translation unit. Per C99 inline rules, an unoptimised C build may fail to link (from reading the code, not tested).

Compiler flags can move performance either way: the author saw -march=native speed up sizes above 2048 but run sizes below 2048 twice as slow, and got mixed results with -ffast-math. The README example (void main(char** argv, int argv), <malloc.h>) does not compile as written.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against the catalogued siblings, muFFT and PFFFT are 3.5-6.5x faster with SIMD in gemmi's run, and PocketFFT (C++ branch) is faster even in scalar code while adding double precision, any size via Bluestein, and 2D/3D. Pick meow_fft only when the constraints are a single 0BSD C99 file and arbitrary 1D float sizes (PFFFT's SIMD path needs multiples of 16 complex or 32 real), and your sizes are mostly powers of two.
verified_claims_summary: gemmi's independent single-precision shootout (1d.cpp, GCC 8 -O3, Intel i7-5600U) timed meow_fft complex FFTs at 2120/4718/5745/4342 ns against KissFFT's 2536/4929/6030/6553 ns for n=256/384/480/512 (1.04-1.51x, derived from page data). In the same run its real FFT was slower at n=480 (3591 against 3140 ns) and faster at n=512 (2660 against 2985 ns). The author's own table (i7-4790, GCC 6.3.1 -O2 -g, benchmark code not published) shows N=1024 at 8.89 against 13.12 us and N=8192 at 84.72 against 119.38 us; accuracy after a round trip was about the same as KissFFT's.
status_note: Stale: 15 commits, the last in July 2024 (real-FFT buffers halved), with two open PRs unmerged, including a 2025 sign-type fix. It is 0BSD and a single header, so it is easy to vendor and patch.
